Claims must match the running site (about_geohub/index.html, data/index.html and the code); edit here and re-run the generator rather than editing the pages.

hub.title: Explore GeoHUB | 3D Planet Viewers, Flight Simulators & Hazard Maps | GeoID
hub.description: Free 3D tools in your browser: fly real Earth terrain or Mars, explore Saturn, Jupiter and Pluto in 3D, and map earthquakes, volcanoes, geology, satellites and storms.
hub.lead: Every tool on one page. They all run in a web browser, with nothing to install and no account: two flight simulators, nine planet and moon viewers built on mission data, and the live maps and records that make up the GeoHUB globe.

image.alt: The GeoHUB globe with world geology and live events over 3D terrain

groups.title: Earth, live and on the record

features.name: Earth Flight
features.title: Free Flight Simulator in Your Browser | Fly Real Earth Terrain | GeoID
features.description: Fly anywhere on Earth over real satellite imagery and real terrain, free in your browser — 3D buildings, real street lights at night, weather clouds and landmarks labelled as you fly.
features.h1: Fly the Real Earth in Your Browser
features.lead: Earth Flight puts a light aircraft or a helicopter anywhere on the planet and flies it over the real ground: satellite imagery on true terrain, OpenStreetMap buildings and trees, and towns and landmarks named as they come into view. No download, no account — open it and fly.

image.alt: A light aircraft flying over forested foothills and valleys in Earth Flight

highlights.title: Real ground, everywhere
highlights.text: Esri World Imagery down to street level, laid on streamed elevation so mountains, valleys and coastlines are where they really are.

highlights.title: A real night
highlights.text: After dark the imagery dims and street lamps appear along real OpenStreetMap roads — lit where NASA's Black Marble satellite data shows a town is lit.

highlights.title: Places as you fly
highlights.text: Cities and towns from high up; villages, landmarks, museums and historic sites as you come down, from OpenStreetMap and Wikipedia. Click one for its card.

highlights.title: Sky and weather
highlights.text: Day, dusk and night follow the real sun over where you are, with high cloud from the day's weather.

p: Choose a light aircraft or a helicopter, pick a launch height from 300 metres to orbit, and take off from wherever you are looking — or open one of the launch points below. The aircraft flies with the planet turning under it, the HUD reads altitude, speed, heading, temperature and pressure for where you are, and names the country and nearest town.
Fly with the keyboard or a game controller. The helicopter is held to its real service ceiling; the aircraft can climb as far as you like.

Earth Flight is part of the GeoHUB globe, so its layers fly too. Switch on world geology, a river network or an Earth Engine image and it is painted onto the terrain under the wings, hidden by the hills like the ground itself, and every feature can still be clicked for its card.

faq.a: Yes. Earth Flight runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

faq.q: Can I fly over my own town?
faq.a: Yes — anywhere on Earth. Look at the place on the globe and launch, or add &lat= and &lon= to the Earth Flight link.

faq.q: What does it need to run?
faq.a: A modern browser with WebGL on a desktop or laptop. The imagery and terrain stream as you fly, so a steady connection helps.

features.sources: Imagery: Esri World Imagery. Elevation: streamed Terrarium tiles. Buildings, roads and place names: © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) via OpenFreeMap. Night lights: NASA Black Marble (VIIRS). Landmarks: Wikipedia (CC BY-SA).

features.name: Mars flight simulator
features.title: Mars Flight Simulator | Fly Over Mars in 3D, Free in Your Browser | GeoID
features.description: Fly over the real surface of Mars: NASA MOLA relief with the CTX image mosaic streamed beneath you, from an 8 km low pass to 300 km orbit, free in your browser.
features.lead: Pick a launch site anywhere on Mars and fly it: the planet's real relief from NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, with the Context Camera mosaic streamed tile by tile beneath you, from a low pass over the canyons to orbit.

image.alt: Flying low over the cratered surface of Mars in the Mars flight simulator

highlights.title: Real Martian terrain
highlights.text: MOLA relief — the altimeter map every Mars landing site is chosen on — under every pass.

highlights.title: Imagery that sharpens as you descend
highlights.text: The CTX mosaic streams beneath the aircraft, so the closer you fly the more of the ground you see.

highlights.title: 8 km to 300 km
highlights.text: Skim Valles Marineris or climb to orbit and watch the planet curve away.

highlights.title: Named features
highlights.text: The places on the skyline are flagged with their names and their range, the most significant first.

sections.h2: A map as well as a flight
p: The flight simulator lives inside the Mars viewer, so the same window has the planet's mapped geology, elevation profiles, named-feature search, a core cutaway and a raster calculator that floods the northern lowlands to test where an ancient ocean might have stood.

faq.a: Yes: it is NASA's MOLA elevation, with Context Camera images streamed over it.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: Relief: NASA MGS MOLA. Imagery: MRO Context Camera (CTX) mosaic. Feature names: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.name: Mercury
features.title: Mercury 3D Viewer | Explore Mercury's Craters & Scarps in 3D | GeoID
features.description: Explore Mercury in 3D on NASA MESSENGER's global mosaic: named craters, basins and lobate scarps, elevation profiles, geology and a core cutaway — free in your browser.
features.lead: Spin, zoom and explore the innermost planet on the global mosaic NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft returned from orbit, with its named craters, basins and the long lobate scarps left as Mercury cooled and shrank.

image.alt: Mercury's cratered surface in the GeoHUB 3D viewer

highlights.title: MESSENGER's mosaic
highlights.text: The whole planet from the first spacecraft to orbit it.

highlights.title: Named features
highlights.text: Search the IAU-recognised craters, basins and scarps and fly straight to them.

highlights.title: Elevation profiles
highlights.text: Draw a line across a basin rim and read its relief.

highlights.title: Core cutaway
highlights.text: Slice the planet open to its outsized iron core.

sections.h2: A shrinking planet, on the map
p: Mercury's scarps run for hundreds of kilometres: cliffs pushed up as the planet's interior cooled and its crust contracted. In the viewer they are named and clickable, beside the great Caloris basin and the craters that cover the rest of the surface.

faq.q: What data is it built from?
faq.a: NASA MESSENGER's global mosaic, with IAU-recognised feature names.
Yes — it runs in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

features.sources: NASA MESSENGER global mosaic; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.name: Venus
features.title: Venus 3D Viewer | Explore the Surface of Venus in 3D | GeoID
features.description: Explore the surface of Venus in 3D from NASA Magellan radar: volcanic plains, coronae and the deformed highlands under the cloud deck — free in your browser.
features.lead: Venus hides under permanent cloud, but radar sees through it. Explore the surface NASA's Magellan mission mapped: volcanic plains, the ring-shaped coronae and the deformed highlands of a planet the size of Earth.

image.alt: The radar-mapped surface of Venus in the GeoHUB 3D viewer

highlights.title: Magellan radar
highlights.text: The surface as the radar saw it, beneath the cloud deck.

highlights.title: Volcanoes and coronae
highlights.text: Named volcanoes, coronae and highlands you can search and visit.

highlights.title: Elevation profiles
highlights.text: Read the relief of a volcano or a highland plateau along any line.

highlights.title: Core cutaway
highlights.text: Open the planet to see its layered interior.

p: Venus is almost Earth's size, yet its surface is young volcanic plains with no plate tectonics. In the viewer the coronae — circular rises where hot material pushed against the crust — and the folded highlands are named and clickable, so you can move from one to the next.

faq.q: How can you see the surface through the clouds?
faq.a: The map is radar: Magellan imaged the surface through the cloud from orbit.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: NASA Magellan radar; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.name: The Moon
features.title: Moon 3D Viewer | Interactive 3D Moon Map with Geology | GeoID
features.description: Explore the Moon in 3D: LROC imagery over LOLA relief, 2,087 named features, the USGS geologic map with 12,000+ clickable units, and a core cutaway — free in your browser.
features.lead: The Moon as NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mapped it: its camera mosaic over its laser altimeter's relief, every IAU-named feature you can search, and the USGS geologic map with each unit clickable.

image.alt: The Moon's maria and highlands in the GeoHUB 3D viewer

highlights.title: LROC over LOLA
highlights.text: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery draped on its own laser-altimeter relief.

highlights.title: 2,087 named features
highlights.text: Craters, maria, mountains and rilles — search a name and fly to it.

highlights.title: The geologic map
highlights.text: The USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon with more than 12,000 selectable units.

highlights.title: Inside the Moon
highlights.text: A core cutaway drawn from Apollo seismology.

p: Turn on the geology and every unit answers a click: what it is and how old. Measure a crater's depth with an elevation profile, find the Apollo landing regions by name, or cut the Moon open to the small core the Apollo seismometers revealed.

faq.q: What data is it built from?
faq.a: NASA LRO's camera (LROC) and laser altimeter (LOLA), the USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon, and IAU feature names.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: NASA LRO LROC and LOLA; USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.lead: Mars on the datasets its missions returned: the MOLA laser-altimeter relief, the Context Camera mosaic streamed tile by tile, the mapped geology, and every named canyon, volcano and crater — with a flight simulator in the same window.

highlights.title: Fly it
highlights.text: The Mars flight simulator runs from an 8 km low pass to 300 km orbit.

sections.h2: From Olympus Mons to the northern ocean
p: Search a name — Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Jezero — and fly to it; draw an elevation profile across the canyon; raise the sea level and trace the coastlines scientists still argue over. Phobos and Deimos open in their own orbital view with their features clickable.

faq.q: What data is it built from?
faq.a: NASA MOLA relief, the MRO Context Camera (CTX) mosaic, the mapped geology and IAU feature names.
Yes — the flight simulator is in the same viewer.

features.name: Jupiter
features.title: Jupiter 3D Viewer | Jupiter & Its Moons Io, Europa, Ganymede in 3D | GeoID
features.description: Explore Jupiter in 3D with its cloud bands and its moon system: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Amalthea, each with its mapped surface features — free in your browser.
features.lead: The largest planet and its moons in one view: Jupiter's cloud bands, and Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Amalthea in their orbits, each opening onto its surface with the features named.

image.alt: Jupiter's cloud bands in the GeoHUB 3D viewer

highlights.text: Watch the Galilean moons circle the planet, then open any of them.

highlights.title: Io's volcanoes

highlights.title: Europa's ice

highlights.title: Ganymede and Callisto
highlights.text: 203 and 155 mapped features on the two largest moons.

p: Each moon opens in its own view with its IAU-named features clickable: Io's volcanic centres, Europa's lines and chaos terrain, Ganymede's grooved terrain and Callisto's ancient, cratered surface — Amalthea too.

faq.a: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto and Amalthea, each with its mapped features.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.lead: Saturn, its rings and nine of its moons in one window. Watch the system turn, then open Titan, Enceladus, Rhea, Dione, Iapetus, Tethys, Mimas, Phoebe or Hyperion onto its surface, with every mapped feature named.

highlights.title: Titan

highlights.title: Seven more moons

sections.h2: A planetary system in your browser
p: Each moon opens in its own orbital view with its IAU-named features clickable: Titan's seas and dunes, the tiger stripes of Enceladus, the two-toned face of Iapetus, Mimas and its giant Herschel crater.

faq.q: Which of Saturn's moons are mapped?
faq.a: Titan, Rhea, Dione, Enceladus, Iapetus, Tethys, Mimas, Phoebe and Hyperion.
Yes, in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.

features.name: Uranus

features.description: Explore Uranus in 3D: the tilted planet and six moons — Ariel, Miranda, Titania, Umbriel, Oberon and Puck — with their mapped surface features, free in your browser.

highlights.title: A tilted system
highlights.text: See the 98° tilt that puts Uranus's poles where other planets have their equators.

highlights.title: Miranda

highlights.title: Ariel and Titania

highlights.title: Umbriel, Oberon and Puck

sections.h2: An ice giant and its moons
p: Everything we know of these moons' surfaces comes from one flyby, Voyager 2's in 1986. The viewer puts those maps in their orbital context, with each named canyon and crater clickable.

faq.a: Ariel, Miranda, Titania, Umbriel, Oberon and Puck.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: Voyager 2 imagery; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.name: Neptune
features.title: Neptune 3D Viewer | Neptune & Triton in 3D | GeoID
features.description: Explore Neptune in 3D with its storms and its largest moon, Triton, and Triton's 64 mapped surface features — free in your browser.
features.lead: The outermost giant, with Triton — a captured world orbiting backwards, its surface mapped by Voyager 2. Explore the planet, then open Triton onto its 64 named features.

highlights.title: Neptune
highlights.text: The deep-blue ice giant and its storms.

highlights.title: Triton
highlights.text: 64 mapped features on the moon with nitrogen geysers and cantaloupe terrain.

highlights.title: In orbit
highlights.text: Triton in its retrograde orbit, in the context of the planet.

highlights.title: Free and in the browser
highlights.text: Nothing to install.

p: Triton is thought to be a captured dwarf planet from the Kuiper Belt, and it is one of the few moons known to be geologically active. Its named features — plains, ridges and the dark streaks left by geysers — are clickable in the viewer.

faq.a: Neptune and its moon Triton, with Triton's 64 mapped features.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: Voyager 2 imagery; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.description: Explore Pluto in 3D from NASA New Horizons: the nitrogen-ice heart, the mountains, and the Pluto–Charon binary in one view — free in your browser.
features.lead: Pluto as NASA's New Horizons saw it in 2015: the bright nitrogen-ice heart of Sputnik Planitia, mountains of water ice, and Charon, its moon, in one view as the binary they are.

image.alt: Pluto and its nitrogen-ice heart in the GeoHUB 3D viewer

highlights.title: New Horizons
highlights.text: The surface from the only spacecraft to fly past Pluto.

highlights.title: The heart
highlights.text: Sputnik Planitia, a glacier of nitrogen ice the size of a country.

highlights.title: Pluto and Charon
highlights.text: The binary pair, orbiting a point between them.

highlights.title: Named features
highlights.text: Search the mountains, plains and craters and fly to them.

p: Before 2015 Pluto was a few pixels. New Horizons found a geologically young surface — flowing glaciers, mountains of ice, a hazy atmosphere. The viewer lets you explore those maps and the Pluto–Charon system together.

faq.q: What data is it built from?
faq.a: NASA New Horizons imagery, with IAU feature names.
Yes, in the browser, with no account.

features.sources: NASA New Horizons; IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

features.description: A 3D earthquake map: 312,500 earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 and above back to the year 1008, live quakes as they are reported, and the seismogram of any quake you click.
features.lead: The merged record of 312,500 earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 and above, back to the year 1008, on a 3D globe you can turn and click — with today's quakes streaming in beside them as they are reported.

image.alt: Earthquakes plotted on the GeoHUB 3D globe

highlights.title: A thousand years of record
highlights.text: USGS ComCat, ISC-GEM and GEM's historical catalogue merged into one layer, M4.5 and above.

highlights.title: Live quakes
highlights.text: Recent earthquakes stream in from USGS with the other live events.

highlights.title: Seismograms in the popup
highlights.text: Click a quake and the nearest station's waveform and spectrogram are drawn, with the P and S arrivals marked.

highlights.title: On the plates
highlights.text: Plate boundaries and active faults alongside, so the pattern explains itself.

p: Draw a study area and sample the record inside it, play it through time, or export it. Members can run the seismic risk model: damaging shaking per year by magnitude, computed from the same merged record, with its method stated beside the map.

faq.q: Where does the earthquake data come from?
faq.a: USGS ComCat, the ISC-GEM catalogue and GEM's Global Historical Earthquake Catalogue (CC BY-SA 3.0), merged; live quakes from USGS.
Yes. The globe, the record and the live feed are free in the browser.

features.sources: USGS ComCat; ISC-GEM; GEM GHEC (CC BY-SA 3.0); seismograms from FDSN stations; plate boundaries after Bird (2003); active faults from GEM.

faq.a: Events appear as NASA EONET and the USGS publish them.
No. It is a view of reported events for exploration and research; use official agencies for warnings.

faq.q: Where is the volcano data from?
faq.a: The Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program; live eruptions from NASA EONET.
The map, the hazard rings and the live eruptions are free; the ashfall model is part of membership.

sections.h2: Screening tools, with the working shown
p: Each model is written up in the Journal so it can be checked and cited. They are screening-level research tools, not a certified warning service. The models are part of GeoID membership; the globe, the records and the live feeds they run on are free.

faq.a: Researchers, students and practitioners who want a first, documented look at a hazard over an area.
The models are part of membership (£49.99 a year); everything they are built on is free to explore.
